<p class="quiz-stem">A storm destroys houses in a village, and the reconstruction is financed and carried out within the same year. What happens to GDP?</p>

<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-2"><span>a) Gross domestic product (GDP)</span></label>

<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-2"><span>c) Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI)</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-2"><span>d) Consumer Price Index (CPI)</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>The GPI combines about 26 economic, social and ecological indicators, including negative ones and the value of unpaid work. </div>
<div class="webex-box quiz-question">
<p class="quiz-meta">Question 2.3 &middot; Based on section 2.2</p>
<p class="quiz-stem">Your neighbour helps you move house, and a few weeks later you look after their cat while they are on holiday. Which of Polanyi’s forms of provision is this?</p>
<div class="webex-radiogroup" id="webex-q2-3" data-answer="[0, 1, 0, 0]">
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-3"><span>a) Householding</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-3"><span>b) Reciprocity</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-3"><span>c) Redistribution</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-3"><span>d) Market exchange</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>Reciprocity is give-and-take between people beyond market and state, for example among neighbours, friends or in associations. To endure, giving and taking must not get too far out of balance. Householding is self-provision within the household, redistribution flows through an administrative centre (for example a tax-financed pension system), and market exchange happens at market prices.</p></details>
</div>

<p class="quiz-stem">Feminist economics often uses the third-person principle to define work. Which activity counts as work under this principle?</p>

<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-4"><span>a) Jogging to stay fit</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-4"><span>b) Sleeping</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-4"><span>c) Cooking dinner for your family</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-4"><span>d) Reading a novel for pleasure</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>Under the third-person principle, any activity that could in principle be done by a paid third person counts as work, whether it is paid or not. </div>

<p class="quiz-stem">Deep-sea fishing grounds are hard to exclude anyone from, but every fish caught is no longer available to others. Which type of good are they?</p>
<div class="webex-radiogroup" id="webex-q2-5" data-answer="[0, 0, 1, 0]">
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-5"><span>a) Private good</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-5"><span>b) Toll (club) good</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-5"><span>c) Common-pool good</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-5"><span>d) Public good</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>Common-pool goods are non-excludable but rival in consumption. This combination creates the risk of overuse that Hardin called the tragedy of the commons. Elinor Ostrom showed that self-organized cooperation within clear boundaries can prevent overuse without privatization or nationalization.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="webex-box quiz-question">
<p class="quiz-meta">Question 2.6 &middot; Based on section 2.4.1</p>
<p class="quiz-stem">Whether a good is excludable is a fixed, natural property of the good itself.</p>
<div class="webex-radiogroup" id="webex-q2-6" data-answer="[0, 1]">
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-6"><span>True</span></label>
<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-6"><span>False</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>False. Excludability depends above all on technical possibilities, societal negotiation and power relations. Water can be made accessible or excludable, and even sunlight could in theory be made excludable (Mr Burns in The Simpsons). So the question is less whether the sun is a public good than whether it is treated as one.</p></details>
</div>

<p class="quiz-stem">Why is a flight often cheaper than a train ride, even though it harms the environment much more?</p>

<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q2-7"><span>d) Because demand for flights is lower than demand for trains</span></label>
</div>
<details class="quiz-feedback"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p>This is a negative external effect: costs are shifted onto third parties such as other people, future generations or nature. Neoclassical economics treats such externalities as exceptions. </div>
<div class="webex-box quiz-question">

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
**Question 2.1** (based on section 2.1.1)

A storm destroys houses in a village, and the reconstruction is financed and carried out within the same year. What happens to GDP?

a) GDP falls, because wealth was destroyed
b) GDP can rise, because the reconstruction is recorded as production, even though well-being has worsened
c) GDP stays the same, because destruction and reconstruction cancel each other out
d) GDP is not affected, because natural disasters are excluded from national accounts

**Question 2.2** (based on section 2.1.2)

Which indicator includes negative factors such as environmental pollution and social inequality as well as the value of unpaid work?

a) Gross domestic product (GDP)
b) Human Development Index (HDI)
c) Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI)
d) Consumer Price Index (CPI)

**Question 2.3** (based on section 2.2)

Your neighbour helps you move house, and a few weeks later you look after their cat while they are on holiday. Which of Polanyi’s forms of provision is this?

a) Householding
b) Reciprocity
c) Redistribution
d) Market exchange

**Question 2.4** (based on section 2.3.3)

Feminist economics often uses the third-person principle to define work. Which activity counts as work under this principle?

a) Jogging to stay fit
b) Sleeping
c) Cooking dinner for your family
d) Reading a novel for pleasure

**Question 2.5** (based on section 2.4.1)

Deep-sea fishing grounds are hard to exclude anyone from, but every fish caught is no longer available to others. Which type of good are they?

a) Private good
b) Toll (club) good
c) Common-pool good
d) Public good

**Question 2.6** (based on section 2.4.1)

Whether a good is excludable is a fixed, natural property of the good itself.

a) True
b) False

**Question 2.7** (based on section 2.4.2)

Why is a flight often cheaper than a train ride, even though it harms the environment much more?

a) Because airlines are more efficient than railways
b) Because many of the real costs, such as climate damage, are not included in the ticket price and are borne by third parties
c) Because train tickets include a tax that subsidizes air travel
d) Because demand for flights is lower than demand for trains

**Question 2.8** (based on section 2.5.2)

A small town has only one supermarket, and all residents shop there. Which precondition of perfect competition is violated?

a) Complete information
b) A large number of suppliers and buyers (polypoly)
c) No preferences for individual suppliers
d) None, the market is still perfectly competitive

**Question 2.9** (based on section 2.5.4)

According to the political-economy perspective in the script, what drives the compulsion of capitalist economies to grow?

a) Population growth, which constantly increases demand
b) The individual greed of managers
c) Competitive pressure that forces firms to reinvest profits, so that capital must continuously multiply (M–C–M′)
d) Central banks, which set growth targets

#### Answers and explanations {.unnumbered}

**2.1** b). GDP measures the market value of goods and services produced, not the losses. Reconstruction counts as output, so a disaster can paradoxically raise GDP. This is one of the main criticisms: GDP ignores social and ecological consequences and says little about actual well-being.

**2.2** c). The GPI combines about 26 economic, social and ecological indicators, including negative ones and the value of unpaid work. The HDI supplements GDP with life expectancy and education. The CPI measures the price level, not prosperity.

**2.3** b). Reciprocity is give-and-take between people beyond market and state, for example among neighbours, friends or in associations. To endure, giving and taking must not get too far out of balance. Householding is self-provision within the household, redistribution flows through an administrative centre (for example a tax-financed pension system), and market exchange happens at market prices.

**2.4** c). Under the third-person principle, any activity that could in principle be done by a paid third person counts as work, whether it is paid or not. Someone else could cook for your family, but nobody can jog, sleep or enjoy a novel on your behalf.

**2.5** c). Common-pool goods are non-excludable but rival in consumption. This combination creates the risk of overuse that Hardin called the tragedy of the commons. Elinor Ostrom showed that self-organized cooperation within clear boundaries can prevent overuse without privatization or nationalization.

**2.6** False. False. Excludability depends above all on technical possibilities, societal negotiation and power relations. Water can be made accessible or excludable, and even sunlight could in theory be made excludable (Mr Burns in The Simpsons). So the question is less whether the sun is a public good than whether it is treated as one.

**2.7** b). This is a negative external effect: costs are shifted onto third parties such as other people, future generations or nature. Neoclassical economics treats such externalities as exceptions. William Kapp argued that the more a system is based on maximizing private profit, the stronger the incentive to shift costs, so externalization is built into capitalism.

**2.8** b). With only one supplier and many buyers, the market is a monopoly, not a polypoly. Under perfect competition, individual suppliers have no influence on the price because buyers could switch to other suppliers. If the preconditions are not met, neoclassical economics speaks of market failure, which justifies state intervention.

**2.9** c). Firms produce to make profits and reinvest them. Firms that do not invest, innovate or raise productivity risk losing market share, so competition creates systemic growth pressure. Institutions reinforce this dependency: credit-based finance presupposes growth, and social insurance is tied to paid employment.

:::
